content: The National Antidote Database was established in 2004 to enhance the availability of antidotes. This online platform, managed by the Pavia Poisons Centre, operates 24/7 and is accessible free of charge to hospitals registered within the national health system. Users are required to input and update their antidote stock information and must take responsibility for the accuracy of the data provided. The database allows for the sharing of antidote availability details among registered hospitals, facilitating the rapid identification and retrieval of antidotes when needed. A color-coded system (red, amber, green) indicates the recency of the last update. The system offers several advantages: (i) ensuring the availability of antidotes, including rare ones, in all hospitals; (ii) providing access to additional doses of antidotes; (iii) improving awareness and management of antidote stocks in emergency departments and hospital services; and (iv) optimizing costs and resources at both regional and national levels. The Pavia Poisons Centre also coordinates antidote supplies in high-risk industrial plants, where occupational health services maintain stocks for urgent use during chemical emergencies. Training is provided to company health personnel on managing chemical exposures. Additionally, the centre oversees the national antidote stockpile for chemical and radiological emergencies on behalf of the Italian government, offering both telephone and direct support for managing exposed patients and training healthcare personnel. In 2010, Thailand launched a national antidote program, establishing both national and subnational antidote and antivenom stockpiles. Distribution and stock levels were determined based on demand, urgency, and treatment costs. Healthcare providers were trained in clinical management and the effective use of antidotes. This initiative significantly improved the availability of antidotes and antivenoms and enhanced the clinical management of poisoned patients. Certain chemical substances with antidotal properties, such as sodium thiosulfate, sodium nitrite, and Prussian blue, may not be available as pharmaceuticals in some countries but can be sourced from chemical suppliers. Hospital manufacturing pharmacies could procure these analytical-grade chemicals and process them into formulations suitable for human use. Ensuring the quality and purity of these chemicals is critical, and pharmacopoeial commissions should consider issuing monographs for such substances. Ethical approval or patient consent must be obtained if a pharmaceutical preparation is unavailable and a non-pharmaceutical formulation is being considered. Lowand middle-income countries face unique challenges in managing poisoning cases and accessing antidotes and antivenoms. Bureaucratic and lengthy importation procedures, economic constraints, and limited convertible currency exacerbate the situation. Inadequate documentation of poisoning cases in healthcare facilities often results in a lack of data to guide antidote procurement decisions. Many countries lack poison centres to collect data, advise physicians, and ensure appropriate antidote use. Limited resources for supportive treatment, such as hemodialysis equipment or ventilators, increase the reliance on specific antidotes or antivenoms that can rapidly reverse toxicity. Poor communication systems and transport infrastructure further hinder the timely delivery of antidotes in emergencies. Proper storage conditions, including temperature, light, and humidity control, are essential during transportation and storage, particularly in regions with challenging climates. Efforts should focus on developing antidotes with longer shelf lives and greater stability under harsh conditions. Poison centres play a pivotal role in national antidote programs. They provide a comprehensive overview of poisoning patterns in their regions, identify necessary antidotes, and analyze data to localize cases. This role is especially critical when hospital documentation of poisoning cases is inadequate. Poison centres should educate clinical personnel on the proper use of antidotes and antivenoms and organize training programs for diagnosing and managing poisoning cases. As centres of expertise in clinical toxicology, they should review and evaluate literature on antidote effectiveness and advise authorities on registration and procurement decisions. They should also encourage the creation of national networks for antidote supply, requiring collaboration with hospital pharmacies and relevant authorities. International exchanges of information can help assess the efficacy and safety of antidotal agents, with data collected in a standardized manner to allow for meaningful comparisons. Poison centres should also update data on antidotes with more recent findings and collect information on medicinal products used for other indications that have proven effective in treating poisoning. Veterinary poisoning is a significant issue worldwide, and poison centres often receive inquiries about treatment. The use of antidotes in veterinary medicine presents challenges regarding choice, dosage, administration route, and availability. Each country should establish a working group with expertise in veterinary antidotes, including poison specialists, veterinarians, and regulatory authorities. Some countries permit off-label use of human drugs for animals, as seen in the USA under the Animal Medicinal Drug Clarification Act of 1994. However, this raises concerns about the entry of these substances into the food chain, necessitating adherence to withdrawal period guidelines. Poison centres should be aware of the most common poisons in their regions and ensure adequate stocks of required antidotes. The principles of antidote development, supply, and use for human poisoning also apply to veterinary cases. At the national level, authorities must ensure the availability of necessary antidotes based on the country's poisoning patterns, particularly those on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines. Including relevant antidotes and antivenoms in national essential medicines lists ensures resource allocation for their procurement and distribution. Mechanisms should be established for the rapid importation of antidotes for emergency use, and special arrangements may be needed for the controlled clinical use of antidotes under development. Simplifying the approval process for generic antidotes could reduce costs. Approval by national regulatory authorities or the WHO prequalification process can expedite registration and ensure quality-assured products. National health authorities should encourage the local manufacture and distribution of unavailable antidotes, potentially providing incentives to pharmaceutical manufacturers, hospital pharmacies, and service laboratories. Exportation of these antidotes could also be promoted. At the international level, establishing a mechanism for the purchase, storage, and distribution of certain antidotes could address availability issues in some countries. Regional cooperative groups for antidote supply and storage could overcome many obstacles. International organizations, poison centres, and toxicological associations could collaborate in this area. A pilot project in the WHO South-East Asia Region, coordinated by the Ministry of Health in Thailand, aims to improve antidote availability through regional procurement and emergency provision. The WHO Model List of Essential Medicines is continuously reviewed to include new antidotes and remove those lacking efficacy evidence. High-income countries could support lowand middle-income countries by transferring knowledge and skills for managing poisoned patients and establishing antidote storage depots. This collaboration could also benefit high-income countries by providing experience in managing less common poisoning cases, such as organophosphate exposure and snakebites. In countries with suitable hospital pharmacy facilities, some antidotes could be prepared locally in cooperation with poison centres, provided quality control processes are in place. Education grants and training courses for pharmaceutical staff in this area would be valuable and could be encouraged through international exchange programs.
